record.original_question: (Well-known problem). Does there exist a finitely presented group G such that G ≅ G × H for some non-trivial group H? The first finitely generated example was constructed in(J. M. Tyrer Jones, J. Austral. Math. Soc., 17(1974), 174–196). A finitely presented group that surjects onto its own direct square was constructed in(G. Baumslag, C. F. Miller, III, Bull. London Math. Soc., 20, no. 3(1988), 239–244).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Does there exist a finitely presented group $G$ and a non-trivial group $H$ such that $G \cong G \times H$?

Recall that a group $G$ is finitely presented if there exist a finite set $X$ and a finite set $R$ of words in the free group on $X$ such that $G \cong \langle X \mid R \rangle$. The group $H$ is non-trivial if $|H| > 1$. Here $G \times H$ denotes the direct product of $G$ and $H$, and $\cong$ denotes group isomorphism.

It is known that finitely generated examples exist (so the requirement is genuinely that $G$ admit a finite presentation), and that there exists a finitely presented group which surjects onto its own direct square $G \times G$. The question is whether the stronger property — being isomorphic to a proper direct product with itself as one factor — can be realized by a finitely presented group.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is listed as a well-known open question in collections of unsolved problems in combinatorial/group theory. A finitely generated example is known (Tyrer Jones, 1974), and Baumslag–Miller (1988) constructed a finitely presented group surjecting onto its direct square, but no finitely presented group $G$ with $G \cong G \times H$ for non-trivial $H$ has been exhibited, and no proof of non-existence is known.

status_evidence.claim: The question whether a finitely presented group can be isomorphic to its direct product with a non-trivial group is recorded among open problems in combinatorial group theory.
